# R392 — installed UR/UMF device-USM pool and physical-free accounting

Date: 2026-10-13 (Asia/Tokyo). Read-only source and official-primary-source audit for the installed runtime used by `main-phase-head-alias-12k-admission-root-v1`. No build, test, GPU, process/service operation, environment probing, source edits, or runtime experiment. Only this report was written. The prohibited `prefill-gemm-only-contract-root-v1/record.json` was not read; environment review was limited to the explicitly named allocator/free-memory settings in the permitted head-alias record. R390 is unchanged.

## Installed binary and matching source provenance

The allowed closed run receipt records these provider hashes, and read-only SHA256 of the current named installed files matches each:

- `libsycl.so.9.0.0-0`: `74243bafb2766fd1a038cf80fd62632b4aad9ecfdc0d3ce8711e4515a93d7008`.
- `libur_adapter_level_zero_v2.so.0.12.0`: `05bcafc4a0d45d33f957f16ffb4ba4776da675e79ade1121b93b94b8549335d8`.
- `libumf.so.1.1.0`: `ebe65269abd5869010ab256375e8663f7a8f8b5453e0be0c78f615eb71581ab9`.

The local SYCL/Unified Runtime build source is Intel `llvm` commit `504366f4b82ff00bbac7b0c956635eed8bc599d8`, described locally as `v7.1.1-dirty`. The Level Zero v2 USM source path is within that tree. The worktree has no changes under `unified-runtime/source/adapters/level_zero` or the relevant parser; unrelated CUDA/HIP files and SYCL matrix-combination code are modified, so the overall compiler source is marked dirty. Binary hash agreement plus no relevant local Level Zero source changes lets this report compare the installed UR adapter to that exact source; it does not make the whole DPC++ installation pristine.

UMF source is the separate vendored FetchContent checkout, tag `v1.1.0`, commit `6c97f3de424fa5d852f2e1c0d8f0dfbbc9b419b6`. The system Level Zero loader is `libze_loader.so.1.32.0`, matching local loader source tag `v1.32.0`, commit `d3b3efbdaa27a0aef9a9812cc8fa4260557c1e7c`. The record names the binary GPU driver `libze_intel_gpu.so.1.17.39395`; it is not an open source commit we can map here. `0.12.0` is the UR adapter SONAME/API version in the installed artifact. UR was built as part of the Intel LLVM source tree, so this audit does not claim an independent UR Git tag/commit.

The recorded run forced loading this exact v2 adapter path. In its recorded environment `UR_L0_USM_ALLOCATOR`, `UR_L0_USM_ALLOCATOR_TRACE`, `UR_L0_DISABLE_USM_ALLOCATOR`, `SYCL_PI_LEVEL_ZERO_DISABLE_USM_ALLOCATOR`, and `ZES_ENABLE_SYSMAN` were unset. This establishes default-config selection in this run; it does not establish an observed pool byte count.

## What the installed Level Zero v2 adapter does with USM

At the exact Intel LLVM source commit above, `initializeDisjointPoolConfig()` recognizes only these allocator control names in this code path:

- `UR_L0_DISABLE_USM_ALLOCATOR` and legacy alias `SYCL_PI_LEVEL_ZERO_DISABLE_USM_ALLOCATOR`: either truthy value returns no DisjointPool configuration. The context then creates a proxy pool, which forwards allocation/free to the memory provider instead of retaining allocator slabs.
- `UR_L0_USM_ALLOCATOR`: optional DisjointPool configuration string. The leading `EnableBuffers` field can be 0 to disable pool creation; the parser comment documents `[EnableBuffers][;[MaxPoolSize][;memtypelimits]...]`. Per-type fields are `<max-poolable-size>,<capacity>,<slab-min-size>`.
- `UR_L0_USM_ALLOCATOR_TRACE`: passed as UMF `PoolTrace`; the default is 0.

No additional environment switch is inferred here. The exact v2 adapter source is in the [Intel LLVM commit's Level Zero v2 USM implementation](https://github.com/intel/llvm/blob/504366f4b82ff00bbac7b0c956635eed8bc599d8/unified-runtime/source/adapters/level_zero/v2/usm.cpp), and pool defaults/parser are in the [matching Intel LLVM parser](https://github.com/intel/llvm/blob/504366f4b82ff00bbac7b0c956635eed8bc599d8/unified-runtime/source/common/umf_pools/disjoint_pool_config_parser.cpp).

With allocator controls absent, the v2 adapter constructs one UMF DisjointPool per context/device/memory type. The exact default Device settings in `DisjointPoolAllConfigs` are min bucket 512 B, slab minimum 64 KiB, max poolable request 4 MiB and capacity four slabs per bucket. Shared ordinary USM pooling is disabled; host and shared-read-only have distinct settings and must not be counted as device USM. `pool_disjoint.c` serves requests above max poolable size directly through the provider. For pool-eligible requests, it takes chunks from slabs; a fully freed slab can stay cached, subject to the bucket's slab capacity. Repeated allocations can reuse those slabs without a matching new driver allocation.

A source-based retained-device-pool upper bound for the defaults is about 56.44 MiB per one `(context, device, Device-USM pool)`: UMF has the 512 B and 1.5x intermediate bucket series through 4 MiB; bucket sizes through 32 KiB retain at most one 64 KiB slab, and larger pool-eligible bucket sizes retain at most four slabs of `max(bucket_size, 64 KiB)`. This is a structural ceiling under the stated settings, not a measured byte count. It excludes other memory types, other contexts, unrelated runtime/driver allocations and physical granularity. The 4 MiB threshold means a 3.8 GB Prefill workspace cannot be retained as one USM pool slab. Under the recorded single Strata Runtime context/device path and default Device settings, the DisjointPool alone therefore cannot explain 897,024,000 B.

A parser comment mentions a 16 MiB overall `MaxPoolSize` default. For this exact v2 code path, unset `UR_L0_USM_ALLOCATOR` returns a default `DisjointPoolAllConfigs` directly; the constructor sets per-type values but leaves `SharedLimits` null. The UMF DisjointPool creates its own `SIZE_MAX` default shared limit when none is supplied. Therefore I do not use the parser comment's 16 MiB as a proven cap for this absent-variable run. The per-bucket capacity and 4 MiB Device max-poolable limit still bound the single Device pool as above. A non-default explicit config can change those bounds.

For pool-eligible `free`, UR asks UMF to free the user chunk. It may simply return the chunk to its slab; that does not call the device memory provider and need not raise driver free memory. When a slab is discarded, or for allocation sizes above the pool threshold, UMF calls the Level Zero memory provider. UR configures that provider with `UMF_LEVEL_ZERO_MEMORY_PROVIDER_FREE_POLICY_BLOCKING_FREE`; UMF maps that to Level Zero's blocking memory-free policy. If allocator pooling is disabled, ordinary device USM deallocation goes directly to the provider. This changes reuse and host/device allocation costs, and may change fragmentation/OOM timing, while preserving the UR free API contract. It does not disable Strata's own queue drain or change model arithmetic. Disabling pooling is a useful separate diagnostic arm, but it is not a production-performance-comparable run.

The UR specification states that `urUSMFree` must wait for prior enqueued commands that may access the allocation. Strata's `gpu::free` additionally drains all Runtime queues before `sycl::free`, so the named Strata-owned frees do not rely on an allocator retaining memory to protect a pending kernel. The provider's blocking free policy applies when the pool calls the provider; it is not evidence that a pooled chunk is returned to the provider at every user free.

## What free-memory reports mean

In this stack, Strata `gpu::mem_info` queries the SYCL `ext_intel_free_memory` device info; the SYCL implementation maps that to UR `UR_DEVICE_INFO_GLOBAL_MEM_FREE`. The Level Zero adapter obtains Sysman memory modules and sums `zesMemoryGetState(...).free` across all root-device modules (for a subdevice it filters to the local module), then caps that sum at `calculateGlobalMemSize(Device)`. Sysman free memory is a driver-reported snapshot of free physical memory across the device memory modules. It is not an allocation ledger for the calling process, and it cannot say whether the bytes belong to an app USM allocation, a cached UMF slab, VMM physical memory, another process, or driver/runtime internals.

The [Level Zero Sysman specification](https://oneapi-src.github.io/level-zero-spec/level-zero/1.19.12/sysman/api/apis/memory.html) defines `zes_mem_state_t.free` as free physical bytes. It explicitly deprecates `zes_mem_state_t.size` because it can no longer reliably track allocatable memory. The [UR device-info contract](https://oneapi-src.github.io/unified-runtime/core/api.html) marks global free memory as an optional-query value; UR USM free contract requires prior commands to complete, but neither UR nor SYCL specifies that a subsequent Sysman snapshot must show exactly the same requested byte count immediately. The current Intel L0 implementation's exact aggregation is in [`device.cpp` at the installed source commit](https://github.com/intel/llvm/blob/504366f4b82ff00bbac7b0c956635eed8bc599d8/unified-runtime/source/adapters/level_zero/device.cpp).

UR's optional USM pool info distinguishes `RESERVED_CURRENT` and `USED_CURRENT`: current source computes reserved from UMF provider `stats.allocated_memory`, and used from the adapter's live allocation stats. Reserved includes coarse backing slabs and direct provider allocations; used is live pool allocation usable size. Their difference can expose pooled slack/retained slabs, but it is still an allocator/provider ledger, not a Level Zero hardware free-memory counter or a physical-page truth oracle. Further, the default *synchronous* context USM pool is `Context::DefaultPool`; the installed UR experimental `urUSMPoolGetDefaultDevicePoolExp` returns the *async* pool, and the L0 v2 adapter reports `urUSMPoolTrimToExp` unsupported. Public pool statistics/trim are therefore not a drop-in query/trim for Strata's ordinary `sycl::malloc_device` pool. The L0 `UR_L0_USM_ALLOCATOR_TRACE` is the directly available diagnostic: at UMF trace level 3, source emits per-allocation whether the allocation came from pool/provider and per-free whether it returned to pool/provider. It can be noisy and perturbs timing; use it only in a separate diagnostic request/process.

## VMM is outside the USM pool

Strata's phase expert-cache VMM path reserves virtual addresses and creates/maps Level Zero physical-memory objects through the SYCL oneAPI virtual-memory extension (`physical_mem`, `map`, `unmap`, `free`). It does not call `sycl::malloc_device` through UR's default USM allocator or UMF's DisjointPool. UMF pool statistics/traces cannot count that owner. Virtual address reservation itself is not device physical storage; physical memory objects are. Any VMM release attribution must pair Strata's `physical_mem` create/destroy and map/unmap receipts with driver free snapshots. Do not add VMM bytes to the USM pool reserved value.

## Consequence for the 897,024,000 B gap

The R390/R391 facts remain unchanged: 12K first GEN succeeded; the 32K second request was rejected by capacity guard before workspace allocation; `fresh_free` fell from 5,319,360,512 B to 4,422,336,512 B after head release, a 897,024,000 B difference. The run receipt shows the actual allocator environment settings above were unset and uses the installed exact binary hashes. Under the matching default source settings, the standard single-context device-USM pool can retain sub-4-MiB chunks in bounded slabs, but that source bound is about 56.44 MiB. Large Strata workspace allocations are above its pool threshold and take the direct Level Zero provider path on free. Thus a claim that the default UMF device-USM pool explains the full 897 MB is contradicted by the configured threshold/slab capacity; a claim that *some* sub-4-MiB slab reuse contributed is plausible but unmeasured. Non-default allocator settings, multiple contexts, other UMF pools, oneMath/runtime/driver allocations, VMM physical memory and Sysman report granularity remain separate possibilities; none is evidenced as the owner of the remaining difference.

A sufficient attribution requires a contemporaneous provider/pool ledger and driver free snapshots at the same lifecycle boundaries, plus a proof that the queried pool/context covers the relevant allocations. The current record has neither. Therefore the 897 MB remains unassigned; do not relabel it as cache or allocator-pool retention.

## Smallest useful diagnostic for Main

Use a separately serialized, otherwise identical **diagnostic** process/request only after the current Main run closes. Capture exact runtime/provider binary hashes and the exact allocator environment at process start. At the existing fresh-free boundary, immediately before first GEN, after first GEN quiesces, and after head lease release, record:

1. Strata `alloc_device` live requested bytes/count, plus separate direct-SYCL allocations and VMM physical reserve/map/live bytes. Include successful allocation and successful free receipts with sizes and owner category; avoid counting VMM VA reservation as physical bytes.
2. Sysman `ext_intel_free_memory` before/after a fixed checked wait, and the raw per-module `zesMemoryGetState.free/size` if the harness can expose them. Use repeat snapshots only as diagnostic samples, never as app-owned byte counts.
3. Separate diagnostic arm with `UR_L0_USM_ALLOCATOR_TRACE=3` to identify `pool` versus `provider` allocation/free for the installed default synchronous USM path. Save only the lifecycle window needed for the question. Do not treat its timings as performance samples.
4. If exact aggregate UMF reserved/used values are required, add a narrow diagnostic hook in the installed adapter/source that reports default **synchronous** `DefaultPool` per Device-USM UMF provider reserved-current and adapter used-current at the same checkpoints. The existing public default-pool getter points at `AsyncPool`; L0 v2 trim-to is unsupported. A default async-pool query or a pointer-to-pool query on one USM allocation would not prove aggregate state for the synchronous default pool.

A matched process with `UR_L0_DISABLE_USM_ALLOCATOR=1` (or this build's source-recognized legacy alias) can test whether slab caching changes the free snapshots, with identical service/model requests. Keep it diagnostic: direct provider allocations/frees alter call count, host overhead, serialization, fragmentation and potentially OOM; no speed conclusion transfers to the default arm. It must retain normal queue-drain correctness and does not by itself establish which freed objects contributed in the pooled arm.

Even this owner ledger has limits: adapter `reserved` is provider-requested bytes and excludes VMM; `used` describes allocator live objects, not physical residency; Sysman is a separate global device snapshot; Level Zero allocation granularity, context/pool multiplicity and opaque driver allocations can keep the columns from summing exactly. Only synchronized deltas with one identified backing object and consistent provider receipts could establish a quantitative owner.
